transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-08 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Johnson (Redwood SE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (Mariner CTO), Priya Singh (Head of ML), Jordan Park (Dev Lead), Sasha Kim (Security)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Mariner Retail's path to first token (TTFT), whether they go self-serve hosted or need a dedicated/private pilot. Discussed free credits, basic POC scope, security requirements (SOC2, VPC/KMS), and success metrics (latency under 300ms median for short queries, cost per 1k tokens).

Topics covered:
- Time-to-first-token / onboarding friction
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency, cost, data residency)
- Security/compliance asks: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs
- Pilot criteria and measurements
- Next steps and owners

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for taking time, I'm Alex from Redwood, I run the west SMB account. Uh, quick intro, we'll, uh, run through your goals and then Maya will jump into perf and hosting options.
[00:10] Tom Alvarez: Hey Alex, thanks. We— we just want to get to something we can ship into our search suggestions and customer chat flow. Fast path is self-serve if it meets data controls.
[00:20] Priya Singh: Yeah from ML we care about latency and token cost; also quantization options if we need to run cheaper on dedicated.
[00:28] Maya Johnson: Cool. High level: Redwood has a hosted API you can get via self-serve with free credits, usually we can get you to first token in under an hour once you have an API key and test prompts. If you need dedicated capacity for predictable throughput or private deployment for VPC/air-gapped, those are separate paths we can scope.
[00:48] Jordan Park: Quick question — what does time-to-first-token mean practically? Like do we need infra changes or just an API key?
[00:54] Alex Chen: Mostly API key + a few config bits. For hosted it's straightforward: you sign up, get credits, point your app at our endpoint. For dedicated you need an SOW and a little setup for reserved pools; private usually involves network work (VPC peering or on-prem image).
[01:12] Sasha Kim: On security, we need SOC2 Type II, SSO with SAML, and keys in our KMS, ideally customer-managed. Also audit logs retention for 12 months.
[01:22] Liam Ortega: Yep we integrate with many KMS providers and we support SAML SSO via our console. For private deployments you can keep keys on-prem; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and bring-your-own-KMS for enterprise tiers.
[01:35] Priya Singh: For model selection — are you recommending off-the-shelf open models or Redwood-curated variants? We want to balance quality vs cost.
[01:42] Maya Johnson: We have a model catalog — recommended defaults for retrieval augmented generation vs chat. For early pilots teams tend to pick a small-family model that gives good quality without enormous cost. We also provide quantized variants for cheaper throughput on dedicated hardware.
[01:57] Tom Alvarez: Understood. If we start with hosted, what does the credit and billing look like — can we get, say, 50k tokens to start?
[02:05] Alex Chen: Yep, we typically grant pilot credits — amount depends on contract but for PLG quickstarts we can grant 25–100k tokens depending on the use case. We'll approve a pilot pack after a quick signup and a brief form about use case.
[02:18] Jordan Park: And how long do credits last? Do they expire in 30 days?
[02:22] Alex Chen: Default is 90 days for most pilot credits; we can extend for enterprise pilots.
[02:26] Priya Singh: On telemetry — can we see token-level cost and per-route latency in the console? We need to instrument to guardrails.
[02:33] Liam Ortega: Yes console shows token breakdowns, traces per route, and you can add tracing hooks. We also export raw usage logs for analysis.
[02:40] Sasha Kim: Clarify: if we use hosted, does customer data get logged in a way that could be accessed by Redwood support? We need assurance on data access and retention policies.
[02:48] Maya Johnson: Good question — for hosted pilots data can be retained for debugging and compliance reasons but access is restricted, and we can enable stricter retention policies or opt-out of retention for enterprise contracts. We'll include our data access controls in the security deck.
[02:59] Tom Alvarez: About latency — our interactive search must keep median response under 300ms for single-turn queries. Can hosted meet that or do we need dedicated?
[03:08] Maya Johnson: It depends on model and region. With smaller models and optimized kernels hosted in the nearest region we regularly hit sub-300ms medians for short prompt lengths. For higher QPS or stricter SLOs dedicated pools give more consistent tail latency.
[03:22] Priya Singh: We anticipate bursty traffic during peak shopping hours, maybe 200–400 qps. Autoscaling is critical. For hosted do you do autoscaling and what about warm-start cold-starts for KV cache?
[03:34] Liam Ortega: Hosted autoscaling is automatic; we also have continuous batching and KV cache strategies to reduce cold-starts. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better predictable response at peak.
[03:44] Jordan Park: For the POC, we'd probably test with our reranking flow plus chat triage. What success metrics should we define?
[03:51] Alex Chen: Good POC metrics: median latency, p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, quality metrics (CTR uplift or NPS or manual evals), and stability over peak traffic.
[04:03] Priya Singh: Are there any limitations on prompt size or streaming? We need streaming for chat with partial responses.
[04:08] Maya Johnson: Streaming supported on the hosted API; prompt size depends on model context window — we can surface recommended maxs in the docs.
[04:17] Tom Alvarez: Regarding model fallbacks: do you have automated fallback to smaller models during capacity constraints? We want graceful degradation.
[04:24] Liam Ortega: Yes routing policies can fallback to compatible variants by policy — region, cost, or latency. You can configure a route to fallback to a cheaper or lower-latency model with preserved interface.
[04:34] Sasha Kim: One more from security — pen test requirements, do you provide SOC2 report and penetration testing summary?
[04:40] Alex Chen: We can share SOC2 Type II and a summary of our third-party pentest; full reports are typically under NDA. Will include in the security packet.
[04:49] Jordan Park: Ok what about integration effort for engineering — approx estimate to get first token in our dev environment?
[04:55] Maya Johnson: If you use the SDK and a single end point, devs can call the API in an afternoon. Getting from that to production depends on routing, auth, and telemetry — usually a 1–2 week sprint for a minimal feature with a rollout plan.
[05:08] Jordan Park: That matches our timeline — 2‑week spike to evaluate.
[05:12] Tom Alvarez: Pricing basics — curious about cost delta running on hosted vs dedicated. Any back-of-envelope?
[05:19] Alex Chen: Hosted is usage-based and simpler; dedicated is committed monthly capacity with lower per-token unit economics at scale. Roughly, if you cross sustained large volume (hundreds of millions tokens/month) dedicated or private is more economical. For pilots hosted is usually cheaper and faster. We'll send a sketch later.
[05:33] Priya Singh: For our ML team, the important thing is to be able to iterate quickly. Do you have per‑token cost estimates for the small family models?
[05:40] Maya Johnson: I'll include some example unit costs and a couple of scenarios in the follow-up.
[05:45] Tom Alvarez: Can we run a quick benchmark — like Maya running our anonymized sample traffic against hosted and share latency and cost?
[05:51] Maya Johnson: Yes, if you can share a sample dataset and expected QPS, we can run a small benchmark in our sandboxes. For hosted we can run representative requests; for dedicated we can do a simulated run on reserved pools.
[06:04] Priya Singh: Data residency — some of our EU customers need EU-only hosting. Is region pinning possible?
[06:09] Liam Ortega: Yes region pinning and routing policies can keep requests in region; for private you can deploy on-prem or in a customer's VPC for strict residency.
[06:17] Tom Alvarez: Sounds good. For the POC we want: hosted pilot with 50k tokens credits, perf benchmark, and a security doc review.
[06:25] Alex Chen: Great — action items we'll capture.
[06:28] Alex Chen: Quick recap — Redwood will: 1) enable a 50k token pilot credit (subject to internal approval), 2) Maya will run a 1k request benchmark on hosted using the sample dataset, 3) we'll send SOC2 + security slide deck and sample pricing. Mariner will: share sample anonymized dataset, expected QPS, and list of compliance constraints.
[06:49] Tom Alvarez: That works. Anything else?
[06:52] Sasha Kim: We'll need the contact for security follow-up — will that be you Alex?
[06:55] Alex Chen: Yes, I'm primary AE; cc me on security emails and I'll loop in our security lead.
[07:01] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone, excited to try the hosted path first.
[07:05] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with notes and the decks.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription accuracy: names and acronyms may be slightly off; timestamps approximate.
